Model Test 05.question: ১) Which is not one of the three principal components of microscopic structure of atherosclerotic plaque?
Model Test 05.exp:
The three principal components of an atherosclerotic plaque are:

  1. Cells — mainly smooth muscle cells, macrophages, and lymphocytes

  2. Extracellular matrix (ECM) — collagen, elastin, proteoglycans

  3. Intracellular & extracellular lipid — especially cholesterol and cholesterol esters

Therefore, necrotic core is not listed as one of the three principal components; rather, it develops as a consequence of lipid accumulation, cell death, and cellular debris.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Atherosclerotic plaque → Cells + ECM + Lipid

  • Fibrous cap → mainly smooth muscle cells + collagen

  • Necrotic/lipid core → lipid + dead cells + cellular debris

Exam Pearl:
Three principal components = Cells + ECM + intracellular/extracellular lipid.

Model Test 05.question: ২) OCD is a.......?
Model Test 05.exp:
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is classically grouped under anxiety disorders in older psychiatric classifications and many traditional exam texts. It is characterized by recurrent intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and/or repetitive behaviors or mental acts (compulsions) that cause distress and consume significant time.

Classification note: In DSM-5, OCD is placed in a separate category called “Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders”, rather than under anxiety disorders. However, for this traditional MCQ, anxiety disorder is the expected answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • OCD → obsessions + compulsions

  • Traditional classification → Anxiety disorder

  • DSM-5 → OCD and related disorders

  • First-line treatment → CBT (ERP) and SSRIs

Exam Pearl:
For this MCQ: OCD → Anxiety disorder (গ).

Model Test 05.question: ৩) Which is a modifiable major risk factor for atherosclerosis?
Model Test 05.exp:
Diabetes mellitus is a major modifiable risk factor for atherosclerosis because chronic hyperglycemia promotes endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, inflammation, and formation of advanced glycation end-products.

  • Increasing age → non-modifiable

  • Male gender → non-modifiable

  • Family history → non-modifiable

  • Diabetes mellitus → modifiable ✅

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Major modifiable risk factors → Diabetes, hypertension, smoking, dyslipidemia, obesity

  • Non-modifiable → Age, sex, family history/genetics

Exam Pearl:
DM = major modifiable risk factor for atherosclerosis.

Model Test 05.question: ৪) What type of psychiatric disorder delirium is?
Model Test 05.exp:
Delirium is an acute organic neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by a sudden disturbance in attention, awareness, and cognition, usually caused by an underlying medical condition, drug, intoxication/withdrawal, or metabolic disturbance.

  • Anxiety disorder → excessive anxiety/fear

  • Mood disorder → disturbance of mood

  • Organic disorder → Delirium ✅

  • Somatoform disorder → physical symptoms without adequate organic explanation

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Delirium → acute onset

  • Fluctuating course

  • Inattention is a key feature

  • Usually reversible when the underlying cause is treated

  • Common causes → infection, metabolic disturbance, drugs, withdrawal

Exam Pearl:
Delirium = acute organic brain syndrome.

Model Test 05.question: ৫) Which is most common primary tumor of heart?
Model Test 05.exp:
Myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults. It most commonly arises in the left atrium, typically from the interatrial septum near the fossa ovalis.

  • Myxoma → most common primary cardiac tumor in adults ✅

  • Rhabdomyoma → most common primary cardiac tumor in children

  • Fibroma → uncommon, often ventricular

  • Lipoma → uncommon benign cardiac tumor

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Adult → Myxoma

  • Child → Rhabdomyoma

  • Myxoma → Left atrium

  • Common site → Interatrial septum

Exam Pearl:
Most common primary heart tumor in adults = Myxoma.

Model Test 05.question: ৬) Thunderclap headache is featured in.......?
Model Test 05.exp:
A thunderclap headache is a sudden, severe headache that reaches maximum intensity within seconds to minutes. It is classically associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), often due to rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm.

  • Meningitis → headache with fever, neck stiffness, altered consciousness

  • Encephalitis → fever, headache, altered mental status, seizures

  • ICSOL → usually progressive headache, often worse in the morning

  • SAH → “worst headache of life” / thunderclap headache ✅

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Thunderclap headache → SAH

  • Sudden onset → seconds to minutes

  • Often associated with neck stiffness, vomiting, photophobia, loss of consciousness

Exam Pearl:
Thunderclap headache = think SAH first.

Model Test 05.question: ৭) In which IHD ischemia causes frank cardiac necrosis?
Model Test 05.exp:
Myocardial infarction (MI) is the form of ischemic heart disease in which prolonged myocardial ischemia causes irreversible myocardial injury and frank cardiac necrosis.

  • MI → irreversible ischemia + myocardial necrosis ✅

  • Angina → ischemia without myocardial necrosis

  • Chronic IHD → chronic ischemic myocardial damage, but not defined by an acute area of frank necrosis

  • Sudden cardiac death (SCD) → unexpected cardiac death, often due to ventricular arrhythmia; may occur with or without acute MI

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ischemia → reversible injury → angina

  • Prolonged ischemia → irreversible injury + necrosis → MI

  • MI is diagnosed by evidence of myocardial injury/necrosis in the appropriate clinical setting.

Exam Pearl:
Frank myocardial necrosis due to ischemia = MI.

Model Test 05.question: ৮) Following Mi which biomarker persists elevated for longer time?
Model Test 05.exp:
Among the given biomarkers, troponin I remains elevated the longest after myocardial infarction (MI)—typically for about 5–7 days, and in some references up to 7–10 days.

  • CK-MB → elevated ~2–3 days

  • AST → elevated ~3–5 days

  • LDH → elevated ~8–14 days

  • Troponin I → ~5–7 days (sometimes up to 7–10 days)

Exam nuance: If the question asks for the longest-lasting biomarker overall, LDH traditionally persists longer than troponin I. However, in modern practice, troponins are the preferred biomarkers for MI.

Exam Pearl:
For “which cardiac biomarker persists longer?” → check whether the question means among traditional enzymes (LDH) or cardiac-specific biomarkers (troponin).

Model Test 05.question: ৯) What type of hypersensitivity reaction occurs in pathogenesis of rheumatic fever?
Model Test 05.exp:
The pathogenesis of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) following Streptococcus pyogenes infection involves molecular mimicry. Antibodies generated against streptococcal antigens, particularly M protein, cross-react with host tissues such as the heart, joints, skin, and brain.

This is classically considered a Type II (antibody-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction.

  • Type I → IgE-mediated; e.g., anaphylaxis

  • Type II → antibody-mediated tissue injury → rheumatic fever ✅

  • Type III → immune-complex mediated; e.g., SLE

  • Type IV → T-cell mediated; e.g., contact dermatitis

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Type Mechanism Example
I IgE Anaphylaxis
II Antibody-mediated Rheumatic fever
III Immune complex SLE
IV T-cell mediated TB/contact dermatitis

Exam Pearl:
Rheumatic fever → molecular mimicry → Type II hypersensitivity.

Model Test 05.question: ১০) Which causes localized alopecia?
Model Test 05.exp:
Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp that causes localized/patched alopecia, often with scaling, broken hairs, and sometimes inflammation.

  • Hypothyroidism → usually diffuse hair loss

  • Hyperthyroidism → usually diffuse hair thinning

  • Tinea capitis → localized/patched alopecia ✅

  • Androgen → androgenetic alopecia, typically patterned hair loss

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Localized alopecia → Tinea capitis, alopecia areata, traction alopecia

  • Diffuse alopecia → endocrine disorders, nutritional deficiency, telogen effluvium

  • Tinea capitis → common in children

Exam Pearl:
Patchy/localized alopecia + scalp scaling → think Tinea capitis.

Model Test 05.question: ১১) Which is not an usual indication of lumbar puncture?
Model Test 05.exp:
Lumbar puncture (LP) is commonly performed for:

  • Meningitis → CSF analysis and culture

  • Suspected SAH → especially when CT is negative but clinical suspicion remains

Parkinsonism is not a usual indication for lumbar puncture. It is primarily a clinical diagnosis supported by neurological examination.

 Important MCQ nuance: Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) is also not an indication for routine LP; significant raised ICP, particularly from a mass lesion, can be a contraindication because of the risk of brain herniation. So the question is technically ambiguous if “raised ICP” is intended literally.

Exam Pearl:
Meningitis + suspected CT-negative SAH → LP. Parkinsonism → not an indication.

Model Test 05.question: ১২) What is the major pathological change in bronchiectasis?
Model Test 05.exp:
The major pathological change in bronchiectasis is permanent, irreversible dilation of the bronchi and bronchioles, associated with destruction and scarring of the bronchial wall due to chronic infection and inflammation.

  • Airway dilation & scarring → correct ✅

  • Airspace enlargement → characteristic of emphysema

  • Mucous gland hyperplasia → characteristic of chronic bronchitis

  • Smooth muscle hyperplasia → associated with asthma

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Disease Major pathological change
Bronchiectasis Permanent airway dilation + wall destruction/scarring
Emphysema Airspace enlargement distal to terminal bronchioles
Chronic bronchitis Mucous gland hyperplasia
Asthma Airway smooth muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia

Exam Pearl:
Bronchiectasis = permanent bronchial dilatation + bronchial wall destruction.

Model Test 05.question: ১৩) Which is not a feature of chronic bronchitis?
Model Test 05.exp:
Pink puffer is the classic clinical phenotype of emphysema, not chronic bronchitis.

Chronic bronchitis classically presents with copious productive cough, airway obstruction/increased airway resistance, and often mild-to-moderate dyspnea initially.

  • Copious sputum → typical of chronic bronchitis

  • Mild dyspnea → may occur

  • Increased airway resistance → typical

  • Pink puffer appearance → emphysema ✅

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Chronic bronchitis Emphysema
Blue bloater Pink puffer
Copious sputum Less sputum
Cyanosis common Relatively pink
Airway obstruction Alveolar wall destruction

Exam Pearl:
Pink puffer → emphysema; Blue bloater → chronic bronchitis.

Model Test 05.question: ১৪) Mesothelioma occurs in......?
Model Test 05.exp:
Mesothelioma is a malignant tumor arising from mesothelial cells, most commonly involving the pleura. It is strongly associated with asbestos exposure.

  • Pleura → most common site 

  • Lung → not the usual primary site

  • Heart → rare

  • Pericardium → very rare

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Malignant mesothelioma → pleura

  • Major risk factor → asbestos

  • Latency → often several decades

  • May present with pleural effusion, chest pain, and dyspnea

Exam Pearl:
Mesothelioma → pleura → think asbestos exposure.

Model Test 05.question: ১৫) Which enzyme is secreted by H. pylori?
Model Test 05.exp:
Helicobacter pylori produces the enzyme urease, which hydrolyzes urea → ammonia + CO₂.

The ammonia helps neutralize gastric acid around the bacterium, allowing H. pylori to survive in the acidic stomach environment.

  • Urease → secreted by H. pylori 

  • Carbonic anhydrase → not the characteristic enzyme tested

  • Hydrolase → broad enzyme class, not the specific answer

  • Ligase → not characteristic

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • H. pylori → Urease positive

  • Urease converts urea → NH₃ + CO₂

  • Rapid urease test (CLO test) → used for diagnosis

Exam Pearl:
H. pylori = Urease-producing organism.

Model Test 05.question: ১৬) Which investigation is done in SAH if CT normal or not available ?
Model Test 05.exp:
In suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), if the initial CT brain is normal or unavailable, lumbar puncture (LP) can be performed to examine the CSF for xanthochromia and RBCs, particularly when clinical suspicion remains high.

  • CT → first-line investigation when available

  • MRI → not the routine first investigation for acute SAH

  • LP → detects SAH when CT is negative/unavailable ✅

  • Blood culture → no role in diagnosing SAH

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Suspected SAH → non-contrast CT head first

  • CT negative + strong suspicion → LP for xanthochromia

  • LP is generally performed after excluding a contraindication such as significant mass effect/raised ICP.

Exam Pearl:
SAH + normal/unavailable CT → LP.

Model Test 05.question: ১৭) Which is preferred investigation for diagnosis of peptic ulcer disease?
Model Test 05.exp:
Upper GI endoscopy (EGD) is the preferred investigation for diagnosing peptic ulcer disease (PUD) because it directly visualizes the ulcer and allows biopsy, especially to exclude malignancy and assess for H. pylori when appropriate.

  • USG → not suitable for directly diagnosing gastric/duodenal ulcers

  • Endoscopy → preferred investigation 

  • Colonoscopy → examines the large intestine

  • Blood culture → no role in PUD diagnosis

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • PUD → Upper GI endoscopy

  • Allows direct visualization + biopsy

  • Gastric ulcer → biopsy is important to exclude malignancy

  • H. pylori → can be assessed by biopsy-based tests

Exam Pearl:
Best investigation for PUD = Upper GI endoscopy (EGD).

Model Test 05.question: ১৮) Most of the meningitis are caused by......?
Model Test 05.exp:
Most cases of meningitis are viral (aseptic) meningitis, especially in the general population. Common viral causes include enteroviruses, HSV, and others.

  • Viruses → most common overall cause 

  • Pyogenic bacteria → cause acute bacterial meningitis and are more severe, but less common overall

  • Fungi → usually in immunocompromised patients

  • Tuberculosis → chronic meningitis; less common

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common meningitis overall → Viral

  • Acute severe meningitis → think bacterial

  • Immunocompromised → fungal meningitis

  • Chronic meningitis → TB/fungal

Exam Pearl:
Most meningitis overall = viral meningitis.

Model Test 05.question: ১৯) Virchow's gland are involved in malignancy og which organ?
Model Test 05.exp:
Virchow's gland/node refers to the left supraclavicular lymph node. Enlargement is classically associated with metastatic gastric carcinoma, although other abdominal and thoracic malignancies can also metastasize there.

  • Stomach → classic association, especially gastric carcinoma 

  • Lung → may involve supraclavicular nodes but is not the classic exam association

  • Colon → can metastasize to supraclavicular nodes

  • Breast → may involve supraclavicular nodes

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Virchow node → left supraclavicular node

  • Classic primary → gastric carcinoma

  • Represents distant lymphatic metastasis

Exam Pearl:
Virchow node = left supraclavicular node → think gastric carcinoma.

Model Test 05.question: ২০) Scabies is caused by.......?
Model Test 05.exp:
Scabies is caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis, which burrows into the stratum corneum and causes intense pruritus, typically worse at night.

  • Mite → correct 

  • Lice → cause pediculosis

  • Fungus → causes dermatophytosis

  • Virus → causes conditions such as warts and herpes

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Scabies → Sarcoptes scabiei

  • Transmission → prolonged skin-to-skin contact

  • Characteristic symptom → nocturnal itching

  • Typical sites → finger webs, wrists, waist, genital area

Exam Pearl:
Scabies = mite (Sarcoptes scabiei).

Model Test 05.question: ২১) Which is not a feature of tuberculous ulcer of intestine?
Model Test 05.exp:
A tuberculous intestinal ulcer typically has undermined edges, not raised edges. The ulcers are usually transverse, particularly in the ileum, and healing may produce fibrosis and strictures.

  • Adhesion between bowel loops → True; due to surrounding tuberculous inflammation.

  • Fibrous healing → True; may lead to stricture.

  • Stricture may occur → True; due to fibrosis during healing.

  • Raised edge → False; TB ulcers characteristically have undermined edges. 

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Intestinal TB ulcer → transverse

  • Edge → undermined

  • Healing → fibrosis → stricture

  • Common site → ileocecal region

Exam Pearl:
TB ulcer = transverse ulcer with undermined edges.

Model Test 05.question: ২২) Signs of meningeal irritation excludes....?
Model Test 05.exp:
Meningeal irritation produces signs due to inflammation and irritation of the meninges:

  • Neck rigidity → characteristic meningeal sign

  • Kernig's sign → characteristic meningeal sign

  • Brudzinski's sign → characteristic meningeal sign

  • Papilledema → not a sign of meningeal irritation; it indicates raised intracranial pressure (ICP). 

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Meningeal irritation → Neck stiffness + Kernig + Brudzinski

  • Raised ICP → Papilledema, headache, vomiting, altered consciousness

Exam Pearl:
Papilledema = raised ICP, not a meningeal irritation sign.

Model Test 05.question: ২৩) Which type of carcinoma produces napkin ring lesion?
Model Test 05.exp:
A napkin-ring (apple-core) lesion is classically seen in colorectal carcinoma, especially in the descending or sigmoid colon. The tumor grows circumferentially around the bowel lumen, producing annular narrowing.

  • Colorectal carcinoma → napkin-ring / apple-core lesion 

  • Gastric carcinoma → may produce linitis plastica, not the classic napkin-ring lesion

  • Anal canal carcinoma → does not characteristically produce this lesion

  • PUD → benign ulcerative disease

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Colon carcinoma → apple-core / napkin-ring lesion

  • Diffuse gastric carcinoma → linitis plastica

  • Annular colorectal tumor → luminal narrowing → obstruction

Exam Pearl:
Napkin-ring (apple-core) lesion = colorectal carcinoma.

Model Test 05.question: ২৪) Which is not a type of necrosis in liver?
Model Test 05.exp:
The recognized patterns/types of hepatic necrosis include focal, zonal, and fulminant/massive necrosis. Intrinsic necrosis is not a standard type of liver necrosis.

  • Focal necrosis → scattered individual hepatocyte death

  • Zonal necrosis → necrosis affecting a particular acinar zone

  • Fulminant necrosis → extensive hepatic necrosis causing acute liver failure

  • Intrinsic necrosis → not a recognized type 

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Focal → scattered hepatocytes

  • Zonal → specific hepatic zone

  • Fulminant → extensive/massive hepatocyte necrosis

Exam Pearl:
Focal + zonal + fulminant = types of hepatic necrosis; intrinsic is not.

Model Test 05.question: ২৫) Which antibody suggests low risk or decreased infectivity?
Model Test 05.exp:
Anti-HBe (antibody to hepatitis B e antigen) generally indicates reduced HBV replication and lower infectivity, compared with an HBeAg-positive state.

  • Anti-HBe → lower infectivity / decreased viral replication ✅

  • Anti-HBs → indicates immunity (recovery or vaccination)

  • Anti-HBc → indicates previous or current exposure to HBV

  • HBsAg → indicates current HBV infection

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

Marker Significance
HBsAg Current HBV infection
HBeAg High viral replication → high infectivity
Anti-HBe Lower replication → lower infectivity
Anti-HBs Immunity

Exam Pearl:
HBeAg = high infectivity; Anti-HBe = low infectivity.

Model Test 05.question: ২৬) Which is investigation of choice in stroke?
Model Test 05.exp:
The initial investigation of choice in acute stroke is a non-contrast CT scan of the brain. It is rapid and, most importantly, helps distinguish ischemic stroke from intracranial hemorrhage, which is essential before thrombolytic therapy.

  • CT → first-line investigation in acute stroke 

  • MRA → evaluates cerebral vessels, but not usually the initial test

  • MRI → more sensitive for early ischemic changes but less available/rapid

  • LP → not routinely used for stroke diagnosis

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Acute stroke → Non-contrast CT first

  • CT → detects hemorrhage rapidly

  • MRI-DWI → highly sensitive for acute ischemia

  • CTA/MRA → assess vascular occlusion

Exam Pearl:
Acute stroke → Non-contrast CT brain first.

Model Test 05.question: ২৭) Lithium is used as......?
Model Test 05.exp:
Lithium is a classic mood stabilizer, primarily used in the treatment and long-term prevention of bipolar disorder, particularly for mania and maintenance therapy.

  • Antidepressant → No

  • Antipsychotic → No

  • Anxiolytic → No

  • Mood stabilizer → Correct 

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Lithium → Mood stabilizer

  • Main use → Bipolar disorder

  • Important adverse effects → tremor, hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

  • Therapeutic drug monitoring is required because of its narrow therapeutic index.

Exam Pearl:
Lithium = classic mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder.

Model Test 05.question: ২৮) Aflatoxin B is related to carcinoma of which organ?
Model Test 05.exp:
Aflatoxin B₁, produced mainly by Aspergillus flavus, is a potent hepatocarcinogen and is strongly associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

  • Liver → correct 

  • Stomach → not the classic association

  • Colon → not the classic association

  • Rectum → not associated

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Aflatoxin B₁ → Hepatocellular carcinoma

  • Source → Aspergillus flavus

  • Contaminated foods → improperly stored groundnuts, maize, grains

  • Risk is especially important with chronic hepatitis B infection

Exam Pearl:
Aflatoxin B₁ = HCC (hepatocellular carcinoma).

Model Test 05.question: ২৯) Loss of previously acquired intellectual function in the absence of impairment of arousal is called...
Model Test 05.exp:
Dementia is a syndrome characterized by a decline/loss of previously acquired intellectual (cognitive) functions such as memory, reasoning, judgment, and language, without impairment of consciousness/arousal.

  • Dementia → loss of acquired cognitive function with clear consciousness ✅

  • Delirium → acute disturbance of attention and cognition with altered awareness/arousal

  • Delusion → fixed false belief

  • Illusion → misinterpretation of a real external stimulus

Exam Pearl:
Dementia = acquired intellectual decline + preserved consciousness.

Model Test 05.question: ৩০) Which drug usually causes Stevens johnson syndrome?
Model Test 05.exp:
Anticonvulsant drugs are important causes of Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS), particularly carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, and lamotrigine. The risk is especially important with lamotrigine and in certain genetic populations.

  • Antihistamine → not a usual cause

  • Anticonvulsant → common drug group causing SJS ✅

  • Antiseptic → not a typical cause

  • Antiulcerant → not a usual cause

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • SJS/TEN → commonly caused by drugs

  • High-yield drugs → anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, allopurinol, some antibiotics, NSAIDs

  • Lamotrigine/carbamazepine → particularly important anticonvulsants

Exam Pearl:
SJS + anticonvulsant → think carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, or lamotrigine.

Model Test 05.question: ৩১) Renal biopsy is indicated if proteinuria exceeds........ daily?
Model Test 05.exp:
Renal biopsy is generally considered when significant or unexplained proteinuria is present, particularly when protein excretion exceeds approximately 1 g/day, especially if accompanied by hematuria, impaired renal function, or other evidence of glomerular disease. Proteinuria in the nephrotic range is ≥3–3.5 g/day, but biopsy is not necessarily reserved for nephrotic-range proteinuria. Lower levels may also warrant biopsy depending on the clinical context. Among the given options, 1 g/day is the most accepted examination threshold for considering renal biopsy in unexplained proteinuria. The exact indication varies with age, clinical presentation, suspected disease, and whether the result would alter management.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • >1 g/day unexplained proteinuria → consider renal biopsy.

  • Nephrotic-range proteinuria: ≥3–3.5 g/day.

  • Proteinuria with hematuria + renal dysfunction strongly suggests glomerular disease.

  • Biopsy is performed when histological diagnosis will influence treatment or prognosis.

Exam Pearl:
Unexplained proteinuria >1 g/day → think renal biopsy.

Model Test 05.question: ৩২) Painless recurrent hematuria usually occurs in.......?
Model Test 05.exp:
IgA nephropathy is the classic cause of recurrent painless macroscopic hematuria, particularly in young adults. The hematuria typically occurs within 1–3 days of an upper respiratory tract or other mucosal infection (“synpharyngitic” hematuria), which distinguishes it from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, where hematuria usually appears after a latent period of about 1–3 weeks. The underlying mechanism is deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes in the glomerular mesangium, producing mesangial proliferation and glomerular injury. Minimal change disease usually presents with nephrotic syndrome, membranous glomerulopathy commonly causes nephrotic-range proteinuria, and SLE can cause hematuria but is not the classic answer for recurrent painless hematuria.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • IgA nephropathy → recurrent painless hematuria

  • Hematuria occurs within days of infection

  • Mesangial IgA deposition is characteristic

  • Common in young adults

  • May progress to chronic kidney disease

Exam Pearl:
Recurrent hematuria occurring soon after a mucosal infection = IgA nephropathy.

Model Test 05.question: ৩৩) Silvery scale is found in.....?
Model Test 05.exp:
Silvery-white scales are a classic clinical feature of psoriasis. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by well-demarcated, erythematous plaques covered by thick, silvery-white scales, commonly affecting the extensor surfaces such as the elbows and knees, as well as the scalp and lumbosacral region. The characteristic scale results from rapid epidermal turnover and abnormal keratinocyte differentiation. Removal of the scale may produce Auspitz sign, with pinpoint bleeding. Eczema can produce scaling but typically has less sharply demarcated lesions and may be associated with oozing or crusting. Acne and taeniasis do not characteristically produce silvery scales.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Psoriasis → silvery-white scales

  • Common sites: extensor surfaces, scalp, lumbosacral area

  • Auspitz sign may occur after removal of scales

  • Koebner phenomenon may be present

  • Nail pitting is a common associated finding

Exam Pearl:
Well-demarcated erythematous plaque + silvery scale = psoriasis.

Model Test 05.question: ৩৪) Which is not a urinary feature of Nephrotic syndrome?
Model Test 05.exp:
The classic urinary findings of nephrotic syndrome are massive proteinuria, usually ≥3–3.5 g/day, with lipiduria and often relatively bland urinary sediment. Hematuria is generally absent or mild, and red cell casts are not a typical feature. Red cell casts strongly indicate glomerular inflammation, particularly nephritic syndrome, such as acute glomerulonephritis. Oliguria can occur in nephrotic syndrome, especially when there is significant renal dysfunction or severe edema. Therefore, among the given options, red cell casts present is the feature that is not characteristic of nephrotic syndrome.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Nephrotic syndrome → massive proteinuria

  • Common urinary finding → lipiduria / oval fat bodies

  • Urinary sediment is usually bland

  • RBC casts → nephritic syndrome

  • Nephrotic syndrome may have microscopic hematuria, but prominent hematuria suggests another process.

Exam Pearl:
RBC casts are a hallmark of glomerular inflammation and point toward nephritic, not nephrotic, syndrome.

Model Test 05.question: ৩৫) Which is the most common cause of Nephrotic syndrome in children?
Model Test 05.exp:
Minimal change disease (MCD) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, particularly in children aged 2–7 years. It typically presents with sudden-onset edema, heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia. Renal function is usually preserved. The underlying lesion is mainly podocyte foot-process effacement, which is seen on electron microscopy; light microscopy appears essentially normal, hence the name. MCD is characteristically highly responsive to corticosteroids. IgA nephropathy more commonly presents with recurrent hematuria rather than nephrotic syndrome. Membranous nephropathy is a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, while diabetic nephropathy is an important adult cause but is not a typical cause of childhood nephrotic syndrome.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Children → Minimal change disease

  • Adults → Membranous nephropathy is a common primary cause

  • MCD → foot-process effacement

  • Light microscopy → essentially normal

  • Usually steroid responsive

Exam Pearl:
Child with nephrotic syndrome = Minimal change disease until proven otherwise.

Model Test 05.question: ৩৬) Which is most common tumor of kidney?
Model Test 05.exp:
Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common primary malignant tumor of the kidney in adults. It arises from the renal tubular epithelium, most commonly the proximal tubular epithelium, with clear cell RCC being the predominant histological subtype. Classic clinical features include hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable abdominal mass, although the classic triad is uncommon and many cases are detected incidentally. Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is the most common renal malignancy in children, not adults. Renal hamartoma and fibroma are uncommon benign renal tumors. Therefore, among the options, RCC is the best answer when the question refers to the most common kidney tumor in general adult clinical practice.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Adults → RCC

  • Children → Wilms tumor

  • Most common RCC subtype → Clear cell RCC

  • Common presentation → Hematuria

  • RCC may produce paraneoplastic syndromes

Exam Pearl:
Most common renal malignancy in adults = RCC; in children = Wilms tumor.

Model Test 05.question: ৩৭) Which is the tumor of undifferentiated cell in nervous system?
Model Test 05.exp:
Medulloblastoma is a highly malignant embryonal tumor of the central nervous system, composed of primitive, undifferentiated neuroectodermal cells. It is the most common malignant primary brain tumor in children and typically arises in the cerebellum, particularly the midline in children. Histologically, it consists of densely packed small, round, blue cells with scant cytoplasm and may show Homer Wright rosettes. Neuroblastoma is also an embryonal tumor composed of primitive cells, but it primarily arises from the sympathetic nervous system, most commonly the adrenal medulla. Astrocytoma is a glial tumor, while neurofibroma is a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Medulloblastoma → primitive/undifferentiated CNS tumor

  • Common location in children → cerebellum

  • Highly malignant embryonal tumor

  • May show Homer Wright rosettes

  • Neuroblastoma → peripheral sympathetic nervous system

Exam Pearl:
Primitive undifferentiated tumor of the CNS in a child = Medulloblastoma.

Model Test 05.question: ৩৮) Which is a cause of UMNL?
Model Test 05.exp:
Cerebrovascular disease (CVD), particularly a stroke involving the corticospinal tract, is a common cause of upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL). Damage to the corticospinal pathway above the anterior horn cell produces characteristic UMN signs, including spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar response (Babinski sign), and weakness. GBS is a peripheral demyelinating neuropathy causing lower motor neuron-type weakness. Poliomyelitis primarily damages anterior horn cells, producing LMN signs. Motor neuron disease can involve both UMN and LMN pathways, but when a single best cause of UMNL is asked, CVD is the clearest answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • CVD/stroke → UMN lesion

  • UMN signs → spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign

  • GBS → peripheral LMN-type weakness

  • Poliomyelitis → anterior horn cell damage

  • MND → may involve both UMN and LMN

Exam Pearl:
Stroke affecting the corticospinal tract is a classic cause of UMN lesion.

Model Test 05.question: ৩৯) Which is not a feature of post necrotic liver cirrhosis?
Model Test 05.exp:
Post-necrotic (post-hepatitic) cirrhosis is characterized by extensive hepatocyte necrosis followed by fibrosis and formation of large, irregularly sized regenerative nodules. The normal hepatic architecture is markedly distorted or lost. Therefore, micronodular architecture is not a typical feature; micronodularity is classically associated with alcohol-related cirrhosis and some other causes. Liver cell necrosis is a key pathological feature of post-necrotic cirrhosis. Bile stasis may occur depending on the underlying hepatic injury, but it is not the defining morphological feature. Thus, among the options, micronodular liver is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Post-necrotic cirrhosis → large, irregular regenerative nodules

  • Extensive hepatocyte necrosis

  • Normal hepatic architecture → lost/distorted

  • Alcoholic cirrhosis → classically micronodular in early stages

  • Post-necrotic cirrhosis is often associated with viral hepatitis or severe hepatic injury

Exam Pearl:
Post-necrotic cirrhosis = macronodular/irregular nodules; micronodular cirrhosis is classically alcoholic.

Model Test 05.question: ৪০) Which is the minimum score of GCS?
Model Test 05.exp:
The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) has three components: Eye opening (E), Verbal response (V), and Motor response (M). Each component has a minimum score of 1: E1, V1, and M1. Therefore, the minimum possible total GCS is 3/15. A score of 3 indicates the lowest measurable level of consciousness on the standard GCS. The maximum score is 15 (E4 + V5 + M6). A GCS of ≤8 is commonly used as a threshold indicating severe impairment of consciousness and may prompt consideration of airway protection in the appropriate clinical setting.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • GCS = E + V + M

  • Eye: 1–4

  • Verbal: 1–5

  • Motor: 1–6

  • Minimum = 3

  • Maximum = 15

  • GCS ≤8 → severe brain injury/coma assessment

Exam Pearl:
GCS ranges from 3 to 15; the minimum score is 3.

Model Test 05.question: ৪১) Psammoma bodies are found in.......?
Model Test 05.exp:
Psammoma bodies are concentrically laminated, calcified structures that are classically associated with meningioma. They result from dystrophic calcification and may be prominent in certain histological subtypes, particularly psammomatous meningioma. Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells and are usually slow-growing, extra-axial tumors. Astrocytomas are glial tumors and may show features such as Rosenthal fibers or eosinophilic granular bodies rather than psammoma bodies. Neuroblastoma may contain Homer Wright rosettes, while neurofibroma is a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor and is not characteristically associated with psammoma bodies.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Psammoma bodies → Meningioma

  • Meningioma → arachnoid cap cells

  • Astrocytoma → Rosenthal fibers may be seen

  • Neuroblastoma → Homer Wright rosettes

  • Psammomatous meningioma → prominent calcification

Exam Pearl:
Psammoma bodies = Meningioma.

Model Test 05.question: ৪২) Which is not a mood disorder?
Model Test 05.exp:
Phobic disorder is an anxiety disorder, not a mood (affective) disorder. Mood disorders are characterized primarily by pathological disturbances in mood, such as persistent depression or episodes of mania/hypomania. Major depressive disorder is a mood disorder, while bipolar disorder is characterized by episodes of mania or hypomania with depressive episodes and is classified as a mood disorder. In contrast, phobic disorders involve excessive, persistent, and unreasonable fear or anxiety triggered by a specific object or situation, leading to avoidance behavior. Therefore, phobic disorder is the clear exception among the given options.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Depression → mood disorder

  • Mania → mood disorder

  • Bipolar disorder → mood disorder

  • Phobic disorder → anxiety disorder

  • Phobia → persistent fear + avoidance

Exam Pearl:
Phobia is an anxiety disorder, not a mood disorder.

Model Test 05.question: ৪৩) Hemiplegic gait is found in.........?
Model Test 05.exp:
A hemiplegic gait occurs when there is weakness or paralysis affecting one side of the body, most commonly due to a stroke involving the corticospinal (upper motor neuron) pathway. The affected leg is typically held in extension with increased tone, and the patient may swing the leg outward in a circumduction pattern to clear the ground during walking. A cerebellar lesion causes an ataxic, broad-based gait with impaired coordination. Parkinsonism produces a shuffling, stooped gait with reduced arm swing and difficulty initiating movement. Pregnancy may produce a waddling gait because of altered posture and pelvic mechanics, not a hemiplegic gait.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hemiplegic gait → stroke

  • Cerebellar lesion → ataxic gait

  • Parkinsonism → shuffling gait

  • Pregnancy → waddling gait

  • Hemiplegia → usually UMN lesion

Exam Pearl:
Hemiplegic gait with circumduction of the affected leg = stroke.

Model Test 05.question: ৪৪) Peripheral neuropathy occurs in....?
Model Test 05.exp:
Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated peripheral neuropathy affecting the peripheral nerves and nerve roots. It typically presents with progressive, symmetrical ascending weakness, accompanied by reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes. Sensory symptoms may occur but are generally less prominent than motor weakness. GBS often follows a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection. Encephalitis and meningitis primarily involve the central nervous system, while cerebrovascular disease (CVD) causes focal neurological deficits through injury to the brain and its blood supply. Therefore, among the given options, GBS is the clear cause of peripheral neuropathy.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • GBS → acute peripheral neuropathy

  • Classically → ascending symmetrical weakness

  • Areflexia/hyporeflexia

  • Often follows infection

  • Common subtype → acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP)

Exam Pearl:
Acute ascending weakness + areflexia = think GBS.

Model Test 05.question: ৪৫) Abnormal perception of real stimuli is called......?
Model Test 05.exp:
An illusion is a misinterpretation or distortion of a real external stimulus. For example, a person may mistake a coat hanging in a dark room for a person. The key point is that an actual sensory stimulus is present but is perceived incorrectly. In contrast, a hallucination is a perception occurring without an external stimulus. A delusion is a fixed, false belief that is not consistent with reality and is not explained by cultural norms. Delirium is an acute confusional state characterized by disturbed attention and awareness, often with fluctuating cognition and perceptual disturbances. Therefore, the correct answer is illusion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Illusion → real stimulus, wrongly perceived

  • Hallucination → perception without stimulus

  • Delusion → false fixed belief

  • Delirium → acute disturbance of attention and awareness

Exam Pearl:
Real stimulus + wrong perception = illusion.

Model Test 05.question: ৪৬) In what type of delusion one belief of having special power?
Model Test 05.exp:
A grandiose delusion is a false, fixed belief that the person possesses exceptional abilities, power, wealth, identity, knowledge, or special status. For example, a patient may firmly believe that they have supernatural powers or are a highly important political or religious figure despite clear evidence to the contrary. Grandiose delusions are particularly associated with mania, although they can occur in other psychotic disorders. A hypochondriacal (somatic) delusion involves false beliefs about having a disease or bodily abnormality. A nihilistic delusion involves beliefs that oneself, the world, or parts of the body do not exist or are destroyed. A persecutory delusion involves the belief that one is being harmed, watched, followed, or plotted against.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Grandiose → special power/ability/status

  • Hypochondriacal → false belief of illness

  • Nihilistic → belief of non-existence/death

  • Persecutory → belief of being harmed or persecuted

  • Grandiose delusions are common in mania

Exam Pearl:
“I have extraordinary power or abilities” = grandiose delusion.

Model Test 05.question: ৪৭) Widespread scale with short duration is found in......?
Model Test 05.exp:
A widespread scale developing over a short duration is characteristic of a drug eruption, particularly generalized exfoliative or erythematous drug reactions. Drug-induced skin eruptions may appear rapidly and can involve large areas of the body. In contrast, psoriasis is typically a chronic disorder with well-demarcated erythematous plaques and silvery scales, although generalized forms can occur. Eczema can produce widespread scaling, but it is usually associated with pruritus, erythema, vesiculation, or oozing depending on the stage. Taeniasis is an intestinal parasitic infection and does not characteristically produce widespread scaling.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Sudden widespread scaling → think drug eruption

  • Psoriasis → chronic plaques + silvery scales

  • Eczema → itching + erythema ± vesicles/oozing

  • Drug eruptions may be generalized and acute

Exam Pearl:
Acute, widespread scaling = suspect a drug eruption.

Model Test 05.question: ৪৮) Hypopigmentation occurs in........?
Model Test 05.exp:
Vitiligo is an acquired depigmenting disorder characterized by destruction or loss of functional melanocytes, producing well-demarcated depigmented or hypopigmented macules and patches. It commonly affects the face, hands, genital area, and other sites, and may be associated with other autoimmune diseases. Addison’s disease classically causes hyperpigmentation due to increased ACTH and melanocyte stimulation. Cushing’s syndrome may produce various skin changes, including thinning and striae, but hypopigmentation is not the characteristic finding. Chronic renal failure can cause pallor or other pigmentary changes, but vitiligo is the clear answer among the options.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Vitiligo → hypopigmentation/depigmentation

  • Addison’s disease → hyperpigmentation

  • Vitiligo → loss of melanocytes

  • Common sites → face, hands, genital region

  • Often associated with autoimmune disorders

Exam Pearl:
Hypopigmented/depigmented patches due to melanocyte loss = vitiligo.

Model Test 05.question: ৪৯) Which is the most common organism of pyogenic liver abscess?
Model Test 05.exp:
Escherichia coli (E. coli) is a commonly isolated organism and the classic most common causative organism of pyogenic liver abscess in many exam settings. Pyogenic liver abscesses are usually polymicrobial, particularly when associated with biliary or intra-abdominal infection. Other important organisms include Klebsiella pneumoniae, Streptococcus species, and anaerobes. Streptococcus milleri (anginosus group) is an important cause of liver abscess and is particularly associated with abscess formation, but E. coli remains the expected answer among the options provided. S. faecalis and S. pyogenes are less commonly responsible.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pyogenic liver abscess → commonly E. coli

  • Often polymicrobial

  • Important organism → Klebsiella pneumoniae

  • S. milleri → important abscess-forming organism

  • Amoebic liver abscess → Entamoeba histolytica

Exam Pearl:
Pyogenic liver abscess: E. coli is the classic exam answer.

Model Test 05.question: ৫০) Gastric carcinoma is associated with which type of anemia?
Model Test 05.exp:
Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is commonly associated with gastric carcinoma, primarily because gastric cancer can cause chronic occult gastrointestinal blood loss, leading to depletion of iron stores. Reduced food intake and impaired iron absorption may also contribute. In an adult, particularly an older adult, unexplained iron deficiency anemia should raise suspicion of gastrointestinal blood loss, including malignancy. Pernicious anemia is associated with autoimmune chronic atrophic gastritis and is a risk factor for gastric carcinoma, but it is not the typical anemia directly produced by gastric carcinoma. Hemolytic and aplastic anemia are not characteristic associations.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gastric carcinoma → iron deficiency anemia

  • Mechanism → chronic occult blood loss

  • Adult IDA → investigate for GI blood loss

  • Pernicious anemia → associated with gastric atrophy and increased gastric cancer risk

  • Gastric carcinoma may also cause weight loss and anorexia

Exam Pearl:
Gastric carcinoma + anemia → think iron deficiency from chronic occult GI blood loss.
